allusions.nt_words: ὅπως ἄν ἐκζητήσωσι(ν) οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τόν κύριον καί πάντα τά ἔθνη ἐπί οὕς ἐπικέκληται τό ὄνομα μου ἐπί αὐτούς λέγει κύριος ποιῶν ταῦτα
allusions.ot_mt_form: Hebrew MT Amos 9:12 reads: 'lemaʿan yîrəšû ʾet-šəʾērît ʾĕdôm wəkol-haggôyim ʾăšer-niqrāʾ šəmî ʿălêhem' — 'so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations over whom my name is called'
allusions.ot_lxx_form: LXX Amos 9:12 reads: 'ὅπως ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ἐφ᾽ οὓς ἐπικέκληται τὸ ὄνομά μου ἐπ᾽ αὐτούς, λέγει κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὁ ποιῶν ταῦτα'
allusions.key_word: ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων / κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων
allusions.textual_implication: The LXX reads 'the remnant of humanity will seek the Lord' where the MT reads 'they may possess the remnant of Edom,' a divergence arising from the LXX translator reading Hebrew ydršw ('they shall seek') for MT yîrəšû ('they shall possess') and understanding ʾĕdôm ('Edom') as ʾādām ('humanity/mankind'). James's citation in Acts 15:17 follows the LXX almost verbatim, and this is theologically decisive: whereas the MT speaks of Israelite dominion over Edom, the LXX (and Acts) speaks of Gentiles seeking the Lord, directly supporting the Gentile mission. The LXX form thus provides the scriptural warrant for the Jerusalem Council's affirmation of Gentile inclusion without circumcision.
allusions.textual_implication_plain: James quotes from a Greek Bible translation (the LXX) that differs significantly from the Hebrew — the Hebrew says Israel will 'possess Edom,' while the Greek says 'the rest of humanity will seek the Lord.' This Greek version perfectly supports his argument that God always intended to include Gentiles.
allusions.scholarly_note: Beale and Carson (Commentary on the NT Use of the OT, pp. 582-583) affirm that Luke/James follows the LXX against the MT almost exactly, and that this LXX reading is not a corruption but a legitimate interpretive variant that serves as James's key hermeneutical pivot for the legitimacy of the Gentile mission.

allusions.ot_mt_form: MT does not include the closing formula 'ποιῶν ταῦτα' directly corresponding to this position; the divine speech formula appears differently in MT
allusions.ot_lxx_form: LXX Amos 9:12 closes: 'λέγει κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὁ ποιῶν ταῦτα' — 'says the Lord God who does these things'
allusions.textual_implication: The closing divine-speech formula 'λέγει κύριος ποιῶν ταῦτα' is drawn from the LXX of Amos 9:12, where it serves as the concluding authentication of the divine oracle. Acts 15:17 abbreviates slightly by omitting 'ὁ θεὸς' (present in the LXX), but retains the participial phrase 'ποιῶν ταῦτα' which has no precise parallel in the MT at this position. This minor abbreviation may reflect James's use of a slightly variant Greek text or a rhetorical compression suitable for oral citation in council proceedings.
allusions.textual_implication_plain: The ending phrase 'says the Lord who does these things' comes from the Greek Old Testament and authenticates the quote as a divine promise, though Acts leaves out a couple of words from the Greek version.
allusions.scholarly_note: Stanley (Arguing with Scripture, p. 153) notes that minor abbreviations in closing formulae are consistent with oral citation practices in Second Temple Judaism and do not necessarily indicate dependence on a variant manuscript tradition.

allusions.ot_mt_form: Isaiah 45:21 MT: 'hăgîdû wəhaggîšû' — the Lord as the one who 'declared and brought to pass' ancient things
allusions.ot_lxx_form: LXX Isaiah 45:21: 'ὁ ποιῶν ταῦτα' does not appear verbatim but thematic resonance with God as the one who accomplishes eschatological purposes for the nations is present
allusions.textual_implication: Some scholars have proposed a faint intertextual echo of Isaianic universalism in the phrase 'ποιῶν ταῦτα,' connecting the Gentile inclusion in Acts 15 to the broader Isaianic servant-of-the-nations motif. However, the verbal correspondence is insufficiently precise to constitute a deliberate citation, and the phrase is more plausibly accounted for entirely within the Amos 9:12 LXX text. The suggestion of an Isaiah echo remains speculative and is not required to explain the text.
allusions.textual_implication_plain: Some scholars see a faint connection to Isaiah here, but this is quite uncertain — the phrase is sufficiently explained by the Amos quotation alone.
allusions.scholarly_note: Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul, pp. 29-32) warns against positing echoes where the volume of verbal correspondence is low; this proposed Isaiah allusion falls below the threshold of confident identification.

summary_technical: Acts 15:17 represents one of the most unambiguous cases of LXX dependence in the entire NT, where the LXX of Amos 9:11-12 diverges substantially from the MT through a double graphic confusion (ydršw/yîrəšû and ʾdm/ʾĕdôm), and Luke presents James as deploying this LXX form as the scriptural climax of the Jerusalem Council argument for Gentile inclusion. The text-critical implication is significant: James's argument is hermeneutically incoherent on the MT but exegetically coherent on the LXX, suggesting either that the Lukan community's Bible was the LXX or that Luke has shaped the citation to align with the LXX for his Gentile-inclusive theological program.
summary_plain: James quotes from the Greek Old Testament (the LXX) in a form that differs from the Hebrew Bible — and it is precisely this Greek version that supports his argument that God planned all along to welcome non-Jewish people into his people.

bibcrit_hypothesis.title: LXX Amos Enables Lucan Gentile-Inclusion Theology
bibcrit_hypothesis.reasoning: The near-verbatim alignment of Acts 15:17 with LXX Amos 9:12 against the MT, combined with the theological stakes of the Jerusalem Council, strongly suggests that Luke either found this citation already in use in Hellenistic Jewish-Christian communities or deliberately selected the LXX form because it uniquely supported the Gentile mission thesis. The hermeneutical move is not arbitrary: the LXX's 'remnant of humanity seeking the Lord' provides the only form of the text that carries prophetic weight for James's argument that Simeon's report (Acts 15:14) was scripturally anticipated. This represents Luke's sophisticated deployment of Septuagintal tradition as authoritative Scripture for a predominantly Greek-speaking church navigating its relationship to Torah observance.
bibcrit_hypothesis.plain: Luke chose a Greek Bible translation of Amos that says something quite different from the Hebrew — and it is this Greek version alone that makes James's argument work, suggesting this was a deliberate and theologically informed choice.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis presents a well-established and textually verifiable case of LXX dependence in Acts 15:17, with appropriately hedged secondary claims.

flagged_claims.claim: Beale and Carson (Commentary on the NT Use of the OT, pp. 582-583)
flagged_claims.reason: The Acts section in the Beale/Carson Commentary is authored by I. H. Marshall; the page reference should be verified, as specific page numbers in this volume are easy to misattribute.

Christopher Stanley's 'Arguing with Scripture' focuses on Pauline citation practices, not Acts/James; the specific page citation about 'oral citation practices in Second Temple Judaism' may be fabricated or misapplied.

flagged_claims.claim: Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul, pp. 29-32)
flagged_claims.reason: While Hays does discuss volume criteria for echoes in this general range of pages, applying his Pauline-focused work to an Acts/Isaiah echo is a stretch and the specific page citation should be verified.

flagged_claims.claim: a double graphic confusion (ydršw/yîrəšû and ʾdm/ʾĕdôm)
flagged_claims.reason: This is the standard scholarly explanation but is stated as fact; some scholars argue the LXX may reflect a different Vorlage rather than translator error, and this should be hedged.

safe_claims: Acts 15:17 follows the LXX of Amos 9:12 closely against the MT
MT Amos 9:12 reads 'possess the remnant of Edom' while LXX reads 'the remnant of humanity will seek the Lord'
The Hebrew yîrəšû ('possess') vs ydršw ('seek') and ʾĕdôm vs ʾādām account for the divergence
Acts omits 'ὁ θεὸς' from the LXX closing formula
The proposed Isaiah 45:21 echo has low verbal correspondence and is speculative
James's argument depends on the LXX form of the text
